questions.q: Why does this lesson compare a pretrained model pulled from a hub to an open-source software dependency?
options: Both are third-party artifacts you didn't create and can't fully verify, carrying the same category of supply chain risk
Pretrained models are always compiled from the same source code as npm packages
Model hubs and package registries use identical authentication systems
Neither a model nor a package can ever be checksummed or verified
questions.explain: A pretrained model or dataset you didn't build yourself is a third-party dependency, just like an npm package or PyPI wheel, and carries the same trust-in-the-publisher risk.

questions.q: What is the specific, documented risk with older pickle-based PyTorch checkpoints?
options: They take up more disk space than safetensors files
They cannot be loaded on Windows machines
Simply loading a malicious pickle file can execute arbitrary code, even before the model is run
They are automatically re-encrypted every time they are saved
questions.explain: Pickle's deserialization design flaw means loading a malicious checkpoint file can execute arbitrary code on the machine loading it, independent of ever running the model.

questions.q: Why was the safetensors format created?
options: To compress model files for faster downloads only
To replace model cards with a different documentation format
To add built-in encryption to every model file
To store only tensor data with no executable logic in the deserialization path, closing pickle's code-execution risk
questions.explain: Safetensors was created specifically to eliminate the arbitrary-code-execution risk that pickle-based checkpoints carry, by storing only tensor data with nothing executable in how it's loaded.

questions.q: What is a model card or dataset card, as described in this lesson?
options: A cryptographic signature that proves a model's weights have not been altered
A legally binding warranty issued by a model hub
Publisher-provided documentation describing training data, intended use, and known limitations
An automated scanning report generated independently of the publisher
questions.explain: Model and dataset cards are self-reported documentation from the publisher, useful for context but not an independently verified guarantee the way a signed checksum is.

questions.q: Which practice does this lesson recommend as a real mitigation against ML supply chain risk?
options: Never using any model or dataset published by someone else
Preferring safetensors over pickle-only releases, and checking publisher reputation before loading a model or dataset
Disabling all logging on the machine that loads a model
Only ever training models entirely from scratch with no external data
questions.explain: Real mitigations include favoring safetensors over pickle-only checkpoints, checking publisher reputation and model/dataset cards, hash-verifying files, and scanning before loading.
